title: Your limb is torn off - now what?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss limb reattachment (replantation), starting with the 1962 case of Everett "Eddie" Knowles Jr., a 12-year-old in Somerville, Massachusetts, whose arm was torn off by a train and reattached at Mass General. They cover the history of microsurgery, toe-to-thumb transfers, free flap tissue transfer, cross transfer surgery, first-aid steps after a limb amputation (call 911, stop bleeding, bag and ice the part without letting it touch ice or water), time limits for reattachment, and regrowing digits using extracellular matrix (pig bladder powder) after a hobby shop owner's fingertip injury. The episode closes with a listener correction about syphilis's history in Europe and the Lewis and Clark expedition.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Chuck having a bug and the show going on, then introduce the topic of the Eddie Knowles story.

segments.title: Eddie Knowles train accident and arm reattachment
segments.summary: Eddie Knowles Jr., known as Eddie, grabbed onto a gravel train in Somerville, Massachusetts, in 1962, was knocked off in a tunnel, and his arm was torn off. Workers and a woman applied first aid, and he was taken to the hospital. Surgeons at Mass General reattached the arm, becoming the first human full limb reattachment, after it had been done in dogs. Blood flow returned within about two and a half hours.

segments.title: How the reattachment was done and its outcome
segments.summary: The surgeons reattached arteries and veins first, then bone using a screw, with nerves and muscle left for later surgery. Eddie regained partial use of the hand. The hosts note that microsurgery was new at the time, first performed in 1960 at the University of Vermont.

segments.title: Microsurgery and replantation explained
segments.summary: The hosts explain that microsurgery uses a microscope and fine suture thread to join blood vessels and nerves a millimeter wide. Replantation can take a full day and each part is a major operation. Early doctors resisted using microscopes, and the technique was developed by surgeons willing to experiment.

segments.title: Toe-to-thumb transfer and free flap surgery
segments.summary: The hosts describe toe-to-thumb transfers developed in the 1960s and free flap tissue transfer in the 1970s, where tissue is taken from a donor site such as the thigh, abdomen, or lower back and reattached with its nerves and blood vessels. They mention a case of fingers being placed under a bicep skin to grow a skin graft.

segments.title: What to do after a limb is cut off
segments.summary: The hosts give first-aid advice: call 911, stop bleeding with pressure or a tourniquet, and place the severed part in a bag, not in direct contact with ice or water, then put the bag on ice. Hospitals should have surgeons ready. Reattachment time is limited; a limb may be viable for six to twelve hours at room temperature, or about four days if refrigerated properly. Muscle degradation is the main concern.

segments.title: Cross transfer surgery and aftercare
segments.summary: The hosts describe cross transfer surgery, in which a lower leg is rotated to serve as a knee joint, and a hand transfer that swaps the thumb and pinkie positions. They say rehabilitation is long and grueling, and that reattached limbs can feel different.

segments.title: Regrowing fingers with extracellular matrix
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Cincinnati hobby shop owner whose fingertip was cut off in 2005; his brother applied extracellular matrix from pig bladder powder and the finger and nail bed regrew. They explain extracellular matrix's role in signaling regrowth instead of scarring, and that this ability fades after early childhood. Iraqi war veterans have been treated with it.

segments.title: Listener correction on syphilis
segments.summary: A listener, Kathleen Pierce, corrects the hosts: syphilis was documented in Europe in the late fifteenth century, before Lewis and Clark. The hosts thank her.

segments.title: Sign-off and website plugs
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to search for replantation and extracellular matrix on HowStuffWorks, contact the show, and visit the website. An audiobook sponsor is mentioned.
